newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: Government urged to boost South Korea stock market.
newsitem.headline: Government urged to boost South Korea stock market.

text.p: South Korea's ruling party and a group of investment trust firms on Tuesday urged the government to take steps to boost the stock market, including delaying sales of government stakes in state-run firms.
Investors welcomed the news but refrained from buying shares until the government's response became clear, brokers said.
"Investors will wait until something actually comes out from the government because they are well aware requests are only requests," said Yoo Nam-gil, analyst at Hyundai Securities.
The composite stock index climbed 1.54 percent, or 10.66 points to 702.83 on Tuesday, but brokers said the rise was mostly technical following six straight days of declines.
Tuesday's closing index was down about 30 percent from this year's highest closing at 986.84, set in May.
Requests by the New Korea Party and the Korea Investment Trust Companies' Association were focused on ways to ease the imbalance between share supply and demand.
They asked that sales of shares in Korea Telecom be delayed until the composite index recovered to surpass 1,000.
The government has said it would sell about 260 billion won worth of Korea Telecom shares to corporations and institutions in an auction on December 12-13.
"If accepted, the delay would become the strongest and most immediate boost to the stock market suffering from a share oversupply," said Yoo.
LG Securities broker Koh Soon-shik also said easing share oversupply and boosting buying power were key points of demand from investors.
Also to ease the oversupply, the association asked that supplies of new shares be kept below one percent of gross domestic product (GDP), against an estimated 2.7 percent this year.
Brokers estimate this year's supply of new shares, including initial public offerings and rights issues, to top nine trillion won ($10.8 billion) for calendar 1996.
Initial public offerings alone totalled 943.34 billion won this year, up from 580.14 billion won in calendar 1995, according to Korea Stock Exchange figures.
The association also asked the government to raise the ceiling of foreign share ownership "at the earliest possible date in 1997".
The government has pledged it would increase the ceiling to an aggregate 23 percent during calendar 1997 from the current 20 percent, but no time frame has yet been set.
The association also demanded foreign investment in local non-guaranteed corporate bonds be allowed in 1997, instead of the original schedule of 1998.
Ministry officials declined to comment on the requests.
